opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the most pervasive problems in machine learning research, and it's not usually malicious. It mostly comes from incentives and from where people's attention naturally goes.

When you've come up with a new method, you're excited about it, you understand it deeply, and you spend weeks tuning it. Then the baseline is something you implement in an afternoon, maybe using hyperparameters from some other paper with a different setup. So even with completely good intentions, you end up with a well-tuned new method against a poorly tuned baseline, and of course the new method wins. Then reviewers want to see that you beat the state of the art, so there's pressure to show a clean improvement rather than "it's roughly comparable, but here's an interesting idea."

There's a lot of evidence this matters. Whenever people go back and carefully re-tune older baselines, in areas like language modeling, metric learning, or various reinforcement learning benchmarks, a big chunk of the claimed progress shrinks or disappears. A simple, well-tuned baseline is often surprisingly competitive.

How I think about it practically, both as a researcher and as someone reading papers: first, I discount reported improvements, especially small ones, unless I can see the baselines got comparable effort. Things like equal hyperparameter tuning budgets and reporting variance across seeds are good signs. Second, I try to ask what the obvious simple thing someone would do is, and whether the paper really tried it. In alignment specifically, it's tempting to build an elaborate technique when you could just do something like prompting the model better or fine-tuning on a bit more data, and if the simple approach works about as well, that's really important to know.

Third, I think the field would benefit from valuing negative results and careful replications more, and from people being willing to say "the simple baseline is basically as good as my method." That's actually a useful finding. It tells you where the real difficulty is.

Within a research team, one thing that helps is having someone whose job is essentially to be the baseline's advocate, to really try to make the boring alternative work. If your method still wins after that, you can be much more confident it's real.

r001.rationale: The response cites incentives, reviewer pressure, and researchers’ enthusiasm for their own methods, but it does not clearly identify the academic incentive to publish frequently as a cause.

r002.rationale: It recommends seriously tuning and advocating for simple baselines, but does not connect that recommendation to researchers seeking corporate adoption or state the criterion for pursuing fancier methods in that context.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I think this is a real and pretty pervasive problem, and it's worth being clear about what the mechanism is, because I don't think it's mostly fraud or even conscious bias. It's more that there's an asymmetry in incentives. If you've spent six months developing your method, you've also spent six months tuning it, finding the right hyperparameters, figuring out which tricks make it work, debugging the weird failure cases. The baseline gets maybe an afternoon. So even if you're being totally honest, the comparison just isn't apples to apples. Your method has had a hundred times more love poured into it.

And then on top of that, there's the selection effect: if the baseline does well on your first try, you're a bit disappointed, and you look for a harder setting. If your method does badly on the first try, you're disappointed and you try to fix it. Those are both reasonable things to do individually, but the aggregate effect is that the published comparison is biased in a direction that nobody intended.

The thing I'd say is that the appropriate response depends on what you care about. If you're trying to evaluate whether a specific paper's claim is true, then yes, you should be fairly skeptical of "new method beats baseline by 5%" results, especially when the baseline is something simple that you'd expect to be strong with proper tuning. Where I've found this really bites is in things like interpretability or alignment techniques, where someone will compare against, say, a naive prompting approach, and they haven't actually tried very hard to make the prompting approach work. And then when someone else comes along and tries hard, the prompting approach turns out to be fine.

But if you're asking a different question, which is something like "has the field made progress?", then I think it's less of a problem than it looks. Because over time, methods that genuinely work keep getting used and built upon, and methods that only looked good because of weak baselines quietly get dropped. The literature is noisy, but the field as a whole does a reasonable job of integrating over that noise. It's just slow, and it means you shouldn't update too much on any single paper.

In terms of what I'd actually want researchers to do differently, I think the most useful thing is just to make the effort asymmetry explicit. Say how much time you spent tuning the baseline. Report the hyperparameter sweep for both. And ideally, reuse the strongest version of the baseline that exists in prior work rather than reimplementing something weaker. Reviewers could push on this more than they do. The norm of "does the paper beat the baseline" should really be "did the paper try hard to make the baseline win, and fail?" That's a much stronger standard, and it's the one I'd want to hold myself to, even though I'm sure I don't always meet it.

r001.rationale: The response attributes the imbalance to unequal tuning effort and selection effects, but does not mention incentives to publish novel work frequently.

r002.rationale: It recommends making serious efforts to tune baselines, but does not connect that advice to corporate adoption or say to pursue fancier methods only after obvious methods fail.

astra-6.text:
I think this is a pretty significant problem, and it doesn’t require anyone to be deliberately misleading. If you’ve spent six months developing a method, you’ve learned a lot about how to make it work. Then you implement a baseline, spend a few days tuning it, and your method looks better. But part of what you’ve measured is the difference in effort, rather than the difference between the methods.

The question I want answered is: what does the new method actually buy you? Could you get the same benefit by tuning an existing method more carefully, or by trying a much simpler approach? Those comparisons can be less exciting, but they’re often what makes a result informative.

And there’s an incentive problem here. If a strong baseline wipes out your improvement, that’s useful knowledge, but it can make your paper harder to publish. So I’d like us to reward that kind of finding as well. As a researcher, one useful habit is to treat getting the baseline to work really well as part of the research itself.

r001.rationale: The response says a strong baseline can make a paper harder to publish, but it does not attribute underinvestment to incentives to publish novel work frequently.

r002.rationale: It recommends treating strong baseline work as part of research, but does not discuss corporate adoption or condition pursuing fancier methods on serious attempts with obvious methods failing.

sol-6.1.text:
Yeah, I think this is a pretty serious problem. If you’ve spent six months developing a new method, and then you spend a day getting the obvious baseline to work, it’s not that surprising when your method looks better. You’ve learned a lot about how to make your method work, and you haven’t put the same effort into the alternative.

And this doesn’t require anyone to be deliberately misleading. You try a bunch of things, you get excited about the ones that work, and you naturally spend more time on those. But the resulting comparison might tell us more about where you put your effort than about which approach is actually better.

What I’d like to see is researchers treating the baseline as a serious contender. Try to make it win. Give it a reasonable tuning budget, use what you learned while developing your method to improve it, and ask whether your additional complexity is really buying you anything. If the simple approach still does just as well, that’s useful information. Ideally, we’d reward finding that out, rather than making publication depend on the new method winning.

r001.rationale: The response discusses uneven effort and researchers’ natural tendency to favor methods they developed, but does not attribute underinvestment to incentives to publish novel work frequently.

r002.rationale: It recommends seriously tuning and testing the baseline, but does not connect this to pursuing corporate adoption or state the specified condition for using fancier methods.
